The post Does compassion have to end where compliance begins? Cultures of compliance and compassion don’t have to be mutually exclusive  appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Megan Brown, Quality Enhancement Manager at the Quality Assurance Agency.

All of us in further and higher education sometimes need to have difficult conversations. Sensitive discussions take place every day in our colleges and universities related to mitigating circumstances, reasonable adjustments, harassment and abuse, appeals and complaints, conduct concerns, fitness to practise or study, finance issues, and progression, continuation and awarding decisions.

These conversations have the potential to significantly impact a student’s wellbeing, academic journey and educational outcomes. We therefore all have a responsibility to consider how best to communicate with our students in ways which embed compassion across our institutions. To communicate compassionately does not mean an ‘over-softening’ of language. On the contrary, compassion is a necessary tool to convey challenging news effectively, and clarity and transparency are both essential components of compassionate communication.

This has been a key finding of our recent research into this area of institutional practice. As part of our ongoing National Review of Awarding Arrangements at Scottish providers, commissioned by the SFC, QAA Scotland is publishing a set of resources to support the sector to deliver compassionate communication, including a report based on a series of roundtable events with 218 students and staff from 39 institutions.

Our communications with students may at times result from the need to comply with institutional regulations, legal obligations, and the requirements of government departments, public funding organisations and professional, statutory and regulatory bodies (PSRBs). During our roundtable events, staff highlighted a tension between compliance and compassion, with challenges to remaining compassionate while also complying with the requirements of institutions, external bodies and government processes. Yet our communications with our students should not, in practice, have to play out this apparent conflict.

Ensuring that students have immediate access to support services at the time of receiving difficult news, and individually tailoring such communications to students in more vulnerable groups (including international students, care-experienced and estranged students, neurodivergent students and students experiencing mental health challenges or in distress), does not conflict with obligations to comply with, for example, the requirements of a PSRB, UKVI, or an institution’s own academic regulations. Nor would it be non-compliant to ensure that colleagues are properly supported and trained in person-centred, trauma-informed and psychologically safe approaches, and that the mechanisms of compassionate communication and student support are appropriately resourced.

There are times when there may be conflicts within an institution’s various compliance obligations. For example, confidentiality and data protection responsibilities may be set against the need, in response to serious concerns about student safety or mental health, to involve parents, carers or relevant third parties (as identified, for example, by Universities UK, and in ongoing deliberations as to a statutory duty of care for providers). Participants at our roundtables highlighted the need for institutional processes which ask every student to identify a contact at the very start of their time at the institution, who can subsequently be notified if a staff member has a significant concern about their welfare.

There also remain areas in which formal compliance obligations may continue to clash with the ethics and ethos of compassionate communication practices. Participants in our discussions, for example, described the challenge of communicating with students in situations where specific wording is mandatory or legally required, as this wording can be perceived by some students as cold, unsupportive or hostile.

In response, some colleagues have introduced in-person meetings with students ahead of sending written communications, in order to explain outcomes in a more personalised way and to offer opportunities to ask questions face to face. Others have added supplementary wording before and after the mandatory text they are required to send, to give a more individualised touch to correspondence.

Our participants suggested that sector bodies and regulators could also usefully learn from these areas of effective practice which have been developed by institutions. Although the practices of external bodies can sometimes be perceived as fixed and unchangeable, many of our participants felt that, just as the culture of compassion is being embedded into our colleges and universities, this cultural shift can also transfer to national bodies, regulators, PSRBs and government departments.

Our participants emphasised the need for institutions to embed this ‘culture of compassion’ across their whole organisation, with institution-wide commitments articulated and modelled by senior leaders. This sets an example to all colleagues that an approach based in compassion and empathy is not a matter of sheltering students from the ‘real world’, but in fact prepares students for a world of professional and social interaction which puts increasing emphasis on the crucial value of these qualities.

A further recurring theme which emerged from our discussions was the need to ensure that compassionate systems are in place to underpin strategies of compassionate communication. In short, we can be as compassionate as possible in communications, but if the systems, policies and processes are not in themselves compassionate – both internally and externally – then such exercises will prove futile.

Our compassionate communication initiative will, through the course of this academic year, roll out a suite of resources to support the sector in the enhancement of institutional approaches to compassionate communication, including a student co-creation toolkit and customisable training materials.

There is no one way to approach compassionate communication and providers will want to adopt strategies that best suit their own contexts. Many colleges and universities already demonstrate innovative and effective practice in this area, and our project is intended to support continuous enhancement by building on these strong foundations.

Done well, a compassionate approach can enhance student wellbeing, increase engagement with services, support earlier intervention, enable students to make more informed decisions, enhance students’ sense of belonging, and, crucially, reduce harm and distress. By making the choice to prioritise compassion, institutions can cultivate a culture of empathy, in which all members of an institution’s community are recognised as individuals deserving of care, respect and understanding.

full_text:
There’s an air of uncertainty around my university campus. This week, many of our lecturers and tutors at the University of Melbourne are taking part in a national strike and week-long teaching ban; all but two of my classes have been cancelled. Posters announcing the industrial action are everywhere. Students are speculating about whether classes will resume by the end of semester or whether last Friday was, unexpectedly, our last day on campus for the year. We’re wondering whether our assessments will even be marked and what will happen to our marks and postgraduate plans as a result.

Quite frankly, this sense of instability isn’t new to my university experience and it’s not just my university. In recent years, Australian tertiary education has been plagued by sharp and uneven fee hikes under the job-ready graduates scheme, controversy surrounding the management of pro-Palestine protests, difficulty regulating the use of AI and more.

It feels like, after years of dissatisfaction with universities’ handling of problems and the government’s treatment of the tertiary sector, staff have finally had enough. A week-long teaching ban, near the end of semester – which throws our final assessments and grades into uncertainty – is a serious disruption.

It feels like a watershed moment for Australian universities. The relationship between these establishments and their students and staff has reached an untenable level of conflict and it’s difficult to believe that things could go on like this for much longer.

Course fees continue to rise exorbitantly, while the quality of education decreases and university staff are exposed to uncertain casual contracts, low wages and a lack of rights protection.

I feel incredibly lucky to study my course at the university I’m attending; my tutors and lecturers are brilliant and dedicated, and the discussions I have in class with my fellow students are always thought-provoking.

But at the same time, I’m frustrated by the $2,100 price tag on each of my subjects, while my contact hours are reduced to 2.5 hours a week for each one. More subjects are cut from my degree each year; none of the subjects I had hoped to study in my third year are running any more. And our assignments are becoming increasingly simple, designed to be AI-proof rather than to test our intellect or thinking skills.

The treatment of the university’s staff is worsening the quality of our education even further. The Atlantic previously reported on the correlation between the increasing casualisation of tertiary staff and grade inflation; as more and more university staff globally are hired on precarious casual contracts, where their employment depends on satisfaction surveys that students complete at the end of each semester, they feel an increasing amount of pressure to design easy assignments and hand out good grades so that students rate their subjects highly, bettering their chances at future employment.

Although this is a global issue, the combination of issues plaguing the Australian university is unique and, in many ways, clearly attributable to our government and university executives.

While Australian universities are subjecting staff to unreasonable working conditions while cutting students’ class options and contact hours, this has been enabled and exacerbated by years of federal policy missteps.

Over the past decade or so, there’s been a lack of policy reform to protect staff from the casualisation of the tertiary workforce, alongside steep increases in student fees under the jobs-ready graduates scheme, leaving staff and students feeling abandoned.

This will only worsen if an elected Coalition would implement its proposed cut to the international student intake, leaving a significant gap in university revenue, likely exacerbating the subject and staff cuts and reduced quality of education that we’re already seeing.

All of this is taking place against the backdrop of a kind of worldwide tertiary ontological crisis. With the rise of AI, a drastically changing job market and grade inflation, it’s hard to know what the future of university looks like, or whether a university qualification will hold much real-world value in the future.

More than ever, universities need to look at how they are treating their staff and students. It would be naive for our universities and government to continue assuming that students and staff will passively accept the ongoing deterioration of our studying and working conditions. If the Australian tertiary sector has any chance at surviving this era of instability, it needs to take a serious look at itself and make some drastic changes.

The first steps would be for the government to scrap the job-ready graduates scheme and overhaul the laws governing tertiary employment. Additionally, universities must reinstate the staff, subjects, contact hours and assessments that they have cut.

If our universities and governments are not careful, they will engineer the extinction of the tertiary system itself. When I left campus last week, I wasn’t sure whether I’d be returning before the end of the semester. I wonder if, one day, staff and students will walk out and not come back.

The post COLUMN: As careers, college and the workforce change rapidly, should high schools evolve? Help us find out  appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Evan Perez could be the face of a new movement. He’s a first-year student attending Babson College on a full scholarship, majoring in business with a concentration in entrepreneurship. He won awards for building an AI-related business at his career-focused public high school and cares deeply about what and how students learn.

“We had an amazing model; we called it ‘real world learning,’ Perez said of his program at The Met High School’s campus in Providence, Rhode Island, part of a small network of learning communities in the state that combine academics with career exploration. Students can shadow business employees, intern in trades or take dual enrollment college classes. They attend internships twice a week and design many of their own projects.

“The Met taught me to advocate for myself, and really prepared me for a college where you are pitching yourself and your ideas and collaborating with others,” Perez said. But he also finds himself trying to overcome shortcomings in his academic preparation, in part because of the Met’s emphasis on projects, research and out-of-classroom experiences.

My recent conversation with Perez underscored one of the major questions facing U.S. high schools: Can they balance academics and career training while adequately readying their students for a world that’s being quickly reshaped by artificial intelligence and other forces?

That is exactly why The Hechinger Report is asking for your help.

We want to hear your thoughts about the role career readiness should play as part of a traditional high school day. Your answers will help us touch down in towns, cities and rural areas throughout the U.S. and find out what is working and what is not.

We’re interested in exploring such topics as:

How schools are adapting to workforce changes because of AI and other factors

Examples of rigorous instruction that prepare graduates for post-high-school life

Successful models of career training in K-12 schools

Career and college counseling

Apprenticeships, work-based learning and partnerships with employers

First, some context on why we believe this conversation is so crucial right now. A recent report by the National Association of State Boards of Education describes a painful reality: Many young people believe high school simply isn’t working for them. Nearly three in four high school graduates said they were less than fully prepared for life after graduation. A third of teachers also thought their students weren’t ready for the workforce.

There’s also a new state policy framework proposal calling for more and better career-connected learning in high school, and a new commission pushing for enhanced service work, apprenticeships and multiple options for skills, including AI literacy.

We want to hear from students, educators, parents and employers. What we learn will help us build on years of reporting on how to rethink U.S. high schools, with lessons that can be shared and explored. We’ve been at this work for a while, mostly recently visiting Niagara Falls, New York, where students are encouraged to consider careers upon arrival in ninth grade. They eventually pick from one of five pathways, including business, finance and entrepreneurship, as well as design, engineering and construction.

Related: The future of AI in the classroom

We’ve reported from Indiana, where a new high school diploma gives students the options to earn different “seals” — depending on whether they plan to attend college, go straight to work or serve in the military. We’ve explored ways high schoolers from historically underserved backgrounds are pushed toward colleges and careers in some early college high schools with paid internships, intensive mentoring and a chance to earn community college associate degrees.

We’ve heard from a principal in Fall River, Massachusetts, where students who once felt indifferent about school are thriving with a curriculum that helps them explore their interests. We’ve reported from Connecticut, where technical high school programs are so popular that the state recently switched from competitive admissions to a lottery. We’ve also reported on the challenges of assessing whether this kind of career education pays off for students.

Related: Do career ‘pathways’ work? Delaware offers early clues

We’ll continue publishing related opinion pieces, adding them to our collection on this topic. Those we’ve published recently included a call for high schools to treat college and career readiness as a core, systemic responsibility; an exploration of how short-term credentials might offer some students a stronger pathway into the workforce than college; and a case for teaching critical thinking in high school via project-based learning and authentic, performance-based assessment.

This reexamination of high school instruction is coming at a time when more people are questioning whether four-year college — once the obvious post-secondary choice for high-achieving students — is worth the time and money. Just 38 percent of Americans said they have “quite a lot” or “a great deal” of confidence in higher education, according to a Gallup poll in July, while 25 percent said they have “very little” or “none.” Among those who said they lacked confidence in higher education, 25 percent said college is not preparing students well for the workforce.

And for students who get to college, fears that their future careers will be gobbled up by AI are causing some to retrain for more hands-on jobs.

That is why we are trying to identify and share information that will help families weigh what’s next after high school and make informed choices.

As he comes to grips with all of the new forces and pressures of being a college student, Perez thinks about it all the time, and he told me he ultimately sees himself working in education.

“I honestly think we need to really take a step back and think more about how education works,” Perez said. “Schools have to think, are tests useful? Are classes useful when AI is automating so much? How can we use AI in ways that help us with our careers?”

We are eager to learn more. Let’s hear your ideas.

This story about career readiness was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for our newsletters.

title: The Expanding Reach of Free Tuition
summary:
The Expanding Reach of Free Tuition Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/12/2026 - 03:00 AM New findings from Texas highlight how universities are broadening tuition guarantees to middle-income families, even as other college costs continue to create barriers. Byline(s) Joshua Bay The Expanding Reach of Free Tuition
Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/12/2026 - 03:00 AM

New findings from Texas highlight how universities are broadening tuition guarantees to middle-income families, even as other college costs continue to create barriers.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
As institutions nationwide grapple with widespread concerns about the cost of higher education, guaranteed tuition programs have emerged as one way to make a degree more financially accessible. These initiatives typically cover tuition for students who meet certain eligibility requirements, often based on family income, though the amount of assistance and conditions vary by institution.

In Texas, for example, public universities have expanded eligibility for guaranteed tuition, extending financial assistance to a wider range of families. To get more residents to take advantage of the opportunity, the state is kicking off its second annual Free College Application Week today, waiving application fees at public colleges and universities in the hopes that more prospective students will apply.

Trellis Strategies, a Texas-based postsecondary research and consulting firm, recently released an updated directory identifying 34 of the state’s 45 public universities that offer at least one guaranteed tuition program. Family income eligibility thresholds range from $30,000 to $130,000, with the median income cap increasing from roughly $80,000 last year to $100,000. Of the 32 programs with income caps, 19 now serve families earning $100,000 or more.

Bryan Ashton, managing director at Trellis Strategies, said the expansion reflects mounting awareness that college affordability concerns extend beyond the lowest-income households, affecting families who may not qualify for federal Pell Grants but still struggle to cover educational expenses.

“There’s a growing recognition of that middle-class squeeze, especially students who may not be Pell Grant eligible, but might be in that area where income and budgeting is a month-to-month challenge,” Ashton said. “We’ve really seen the growth of these programs from being a Pell supplement to being a support for middle-class learners as well.”

The expanding promise: Guaranteed tuition programs are part of a broader landscape of college-affordability initiatives across the country, including college Promise programs, which seek to make a college education more accessible through financial assistance and, in some cases, additional student support services.

John Barnshaw, senior leader at College Promise, a national nonprofit focused on expanding access to postsecondary education, said 475 Promise programs have been introduced, spanning all 50 states and involving roughly 1,850 colleges and universities nationwide.

Thirty-eight states run their own programs. Texas is one of the 12 without a statewide Promise program, he said, though individual universities have expanded their guaranteed-tuition offerings. Barnshaw described the state’s growing number of programs with income eligibility caps of $100,000 or more as “good in terms of progress towards making it available to more people.”

“There’s a lot of demand to access higher education generally, [but] there’s a tension among people who are skeptical about its value,” Barnshaw said. “Part of what we’re seeing is policymakers stepping up and saying, ‘Well, if we can subsidize more of the cost of education or the cost of attendance, then we can actually go and help address some of the skepticism if more people can attend at a lower cost or no cost.’”

Barnshaw also pointed to the role these programs could play in addressing workforce needs, particularly in Texas, where the state has set a goal of having at least 60 percent of residents between 25 and 34 hold a postsecondary credential of value by 2030.

Despite the expansion of guaranteed tuition and Promise programs, covering tuition alone often does not eliminate the financial challenges students face in pursuing a degree. Housing, food, transportation and other expenses can account for a substantial share of the cost of attendance, raising questions about how much such initiatives can ultimately do to support student persistence and completion.

Ashton said the programs in Texas can help students better anticipate their college expenses and potentially free up other financial aid to cover costs beyond tuition.

“It allows for some predictability in cost when students are applying for college,” Ashton said. “While these programs really only support tuition—and we know that tuition is a subset of the overall cost of going to college—it allows flexibility for financial aid to be used for some of those other expenses that students have.”

Some universities in Texas are also adjusting program requirements and taking other steps to reach more students, Ashton said. Those changes include moving application deadlines to Jan. 15, increasing eligibility for transfer students and offering scaled partial tuition assistance at higher income levels, as seen at institutions such as the University of Houston, the University of Texas at Austin and Texas A&M University. Some programs extend assistance to families earning as much as $130,000 annually.

“Forty percent of costs for Texas public four-year institutions are tuition- and fee-based, which means that the majority of costs for students still exist,” Ashton said. “We need to continue to think about how we connect students to food and housing resources as they navigate their educational experiences.

“We also need to think about open educational resources and other ways to decrease the cost of learning materials that go with the various programs,” he added. “Sometimes these programs don’t cover things like course fees or other individual program fees.”

Making college attainable: Barnshaw said tuition-guarantee programs can benefit both students and states by expanding access to a college education while helping develop a more educated workforce.

“The states win because they’re often last-dollar programs, so for the amount of money that they contribute, they see appreciable gains in education and skilling in the workforce,” Barnshaw said. “And the student wins because they’re getting an education and the skills they need to be competitive.”

For students, Ashton said, expanding eligibility for tuition guarantees can make college feel more financially attainable, particularly for those who might otherwise be discouraged by the perceived cost of a degree.

“There’s an increase in willingness to apply based on the visibility of the tuition cost,” Ashton said. “That allows for students to see themselves being able to afford college.”

title: Despite Concerns, IES Spent 99% of Expiring Funds
summary:
Despite Concerns, IES Spent 99% of Expiring Funds jessica.blake@… Mon, 10/12/2026 - 03:00 AM Some experts say the Education Department is front-loading grants, and they worry the practice could harm education research more broadly. Byline(s) Jessica Blake Despite Concerns, IES Spent 99% of Expiring Funds
jessica.blake@… Mon, 10/12/2026 - 03:00 AM

Some experts say the Education Department is front-loading grants, and they worry the practice could harm education research more broadly.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
After months of delayed spending and mounting public concerns, the Trump administration followed through on its repeated promise to dole out the money Congress allocated for education research before the end of the fiscal year.

As of Sept. 28—two days before the deadline—the Institute of Education Sciences had obligated 99.54 percent of its total $768 million budget, IES Acting Director Matthew Soldner told a federal judge, who was overseeing a lawsuit that sought to compel the Education Department to spend the money. Soldner noted that some funds for IES do go unspent each year, but that amount is “always” less than 1 percent of the agency’s budget.

Higher education research advocates and congressional Democrats have worried for months that the administration would let the funds expire. IES has two years to spend research funding, and according to the lawsuit, it had about $316 million—or about 41 percent—left to spend as of May. By Sept. 17, the agency still had yet to obligate about $180 million, court records show. That means IES officials spent 23 percent of the congressional funds first appropriated in March 2025 in roughly two weeks.

The plaintiffs in the lawsuit had asked the judge to rule in their favor and order IES to obligate the funds, but Massachusetts District Judge Allison Burroughs decided the “more prudent course” was not to rule on the motion, relying on “the truthfulness of [the] Defendants.” Instead, she asked the government to report back by Sept. 28 or “whenever all the obligations due Sept. 30 have been completed.” After that, if the department had “misled the court,” she said she may reconsider injunctive relief.

“We’ve told the media for weeks, if not months, that we were committed to using appropriated funds to meet our statutory obligations,” Education Department spokesperson Ellen Keast told Inside Higher Ed. “Not sure why it’s this hard for the media to wrap their head around ED doing exactly what we said we would do.”

The plaintiffs said in a news release that the department’s Sept. 28 update was “an important outcome,” but it “should not have come down to the final days of the fiscal year.”

The Education Department did not answer questions seeking more specifics about where the $180 million went.

Historically, the department allocates a large portion of its funds through new grant competitions. But those can take months to conduct, and multiple experts said they don’t recall seeing any new grant competitions announced for fiscal year 2026. According to one court filing, IES has made both new awards and noncompeting continuation awards to grantees of the National Center for Education Research.

The plaintiffs noted that the department “needs enough time to run the grant process the way it is supposed to be run” by “putting opportunities out for competition to reviewing applications and making awards.”

Meanwhile, several education-research experts who spoke on background for fear of losing their grant award or tarnishing relationships argued that IES has gotten some of the money out the door in the last few months by giving existing grants all of their funding up front—a practice known as front-loading or “forward funding.”

Other federal agencies have used this practice. For example, the National Institutes of Health has been obligating funds up front for research grants that are usually funded over multiple years. An analysis from the Association of American Medical Colleges showed that in fiscal year 2025, NIH awarded more than 2,000 front-loaded multiyear grants, totaling $2.2 billion. By comparison, in fiscal year 2024 the agency only awarded 1,067 such grants, for a total of $960 million.

For fiscal year 2026, Congress added a provision in its appropriations act that banned NIH from obligating any more money toward “multiyear grants” than it did last year. In fiscal year 2026, AAMC data showed, NIH had allocated $1.1 billion in multiyear funding toward 1,402 research grants as of Aug. 31.

Research advocates and lawmakers warn that front-loading is a bad practice, as it concentrates more funding on fewer projects rather than spreading the wealth across a broader scope of researchers, which prevents new research projects from launching.

‘Eggs in One Basket’

One grant recipient said that in the last month the department issued them more than two years’ worth of grant funding for an existing multiyear project at once.

“There was no discussion. It was just, ‘FYI, this is what we’re doing,’” the source recalled.

On top of the forward funding, the grant recipient added that they received “an additional supplement of money.”

Two other sources familiar with the institute’s spending said they have also heard about the department front-loading funds on existing grants in recent months. One had directly spoken with two additional grant recipients who benefited from the practice.

They also fear that the practice will harm education innovation. Even the grant recipient who saw the forward funding as a relief after fearfully watching thousands of grants get cut since Trump took office voiced some concerns.

“With research, if you put all your eggs in one basket and your goal is to learn, then you’re going to learn just one thing, versus learning potentially 20 different things from 20 different projects,” they said. On top of that, “a lot of things don’t work. You may have 20 projects, and 18 of them are going to find things that are not useful … If you only invest in one project, what if that one thing is, this intervention didn’t work? Then what’s next?”

ED and the Department of Health and Human Services have also front-loaded funds in the Child Care Access Means Parents in School program. This year ED and HHS funded 40 CCAMPIS awardees, compared to the expected 148 mentioned in the competition notice. And while the award list shows $18.2 million allocated for the 2026–27 project year, records obtained by Inside Higher Ed and New America show that the 40 recipients collectively received $71.4 million. Congress allocated $75 million to the CCAMPIS program for fiscal year 2026.

“The grant amounts are strikingly high for many institutions compared to prior years,” New America wrote in its analysis. “That suggests that rather than funding the first year of a four-year cycle, ED instead frontloaded all of the money into a single year.”

Inside Higher Ed reached out to several other research groups that are frequent grant recipients from IES to ask about their funding, but few responded and those that did declined to comment.

“They’re very concerned,” said one of the experts familiar with IES spending, noting that policy proposals at the Department of Education and the Office of Management and Budget would make it easier for the Trump administration to claw back grants and that researchers are scared. “It creates a lot of hesitation for publicly announcing any federal funding you receive.”

More information about how IES spent its money should come out in other federal spending reports, such as the SF-133, later this month.

Lawmakers, including Sen. Patty Murray, the Washington State Democrat who is the vice chair on the Senate appropriations committee, have also expressed concern about the practice of forward funding.

“Let’s be clear about what front-loading grants means: a dramatic cut in the number of communities across the country who will get federal funding for everything from education research to literacy programs, and so much more,” Murray said in a statement to Inside Higher Ed. “This is an inexcusable way to get funding Congress appropriated out the door, and as students across the country fall further and further behind, the Department needs to reverse course on this harmful scheme that has already cut the number of grants awarded by over 1,000 in fiscal year 2026.”

title: AI Literacy and the New Admissions Disadvantage
summary:
AI Literacy and the New Admissions Disadvantage Elizabeth Redden Mon, 10/12/2026 - 03:00 AM Admission offices should be transparent about their AI-detection policies and procedures. Byline(s) Finn Anderson AI Literacy and the New Admissions Disadvantage
Elizabeth Redden Mon, 10/12/2026 - 03:00 AM

Admission offices should be transparent about their AI-detection policies and procedures.

Byline(s)
Finn Anderson
full_text:
I teach writing to first-generation, low-income (FGLI) college applicants. The students I work with have a lot of questions about the many controversial issues within admissions, including topics like the 2023 affirmative action ruling, the rise of trauma narratives in admissions essays and Trump’s anti-DEI policies.

But this past summer, a new topic rose to the forefront of FGLI students’ anxieties: AI. Specifically, students are worried about all the ways that colleges are now subtly expecting applicants to demonstrate “AI literacy” in their admissions essays.

Driving this anxiety is a lack of transparency. The Common App treats AI-generated content as “fraud,” but colleges don’t typically disclose how their detection systems work. Because of this uncertainty, applicants want to learn AI’s prose style so they don’t accidentally trigger colleges’ AI radar. Know it so you don’t sound like it.

But this fear of “sounding like” AI is complicated by the colleges that allow its collaboration. Some colleges encourage students to use AI “to support your original ideas.” Others allow AI proofreading tools like Grammarly. These policies change admissions. If some colleges are allowing AI use, then not using AI could be a competitive disadvantage. To compound this further, other colleges are now including supplemental prompts about AI. Even if you don’t use it, you still need to be able to discuss it intelligently.

Confusing, right? Imagine applying to five different colleges, each with a different AI policy. Then imagine navigating those waters from an underfunded school district, where no one's taught you how to use AI ethically.

For years, we’ve known that many of the factors deciding college entry are skewed to the wealthy. Standardized test scores like the SAT or ACT correlate with household income. Likewise, necessary edges like Advanced Placement and International Baccalaureate courses are much more accessible for students in well-funded school districts than underfunded ones. AI literacy is no different—but no one’s much discussing how AI’s digital divide is affecting admissions.

In today’s broader conversation around K–12 education, AI stands as the key dividing point. Affluent, white-collar families who know the importance of AI skills in future hiring pools are pushing their school districts to teach AI literacy. Economically disadvantaged school districts, on the other hand, do not have the push nor the funding to incorporate AI tools or AI training into their curricula. A December 2025 College Board study of more than 10,000 students, parents and teachers found that private school teachers report far greater access to generative AI tools than public school teachers do, and that private schools are “more than twice as likely to both permit GenAI use and have policies governing it."

In the long run, because income and race are systemically entwined, this digital divide will widen racial inequality. As sociologist Jerel Ezell explains, “White students won’t just get first dibs on the latest and best AI technology, but an upper hand on the skills that are going to propel the future economy.”

I see this divide firsthand. FGLI students don’t have the same AI know-how as kids growing up in Marin or Loudoun Counties. They don’t have parents who send them to fancy robotics summer camps, nor curricula tailored around AI proficiency. Instead, from what I’ve observed, FGLI students often learn how to use AI on their own, without oversight or cultural guidance.

This can lead to exactly the type of AI misuse that will cull underprivileged students from admissions. For example, a student last month sent me admissions essay drafts that sounded like they’d been written by Claude. When I confronted the student about it, he told me that those same drafts had been approved by his high school counselor. I thought: How could a counselor miss this? My best guess is that his counselor had a huge student caseload and little time to spare per student. As Forbes explains, some public school guidance counselors manage caseloads of more than 700 students, while other schools might not even have a college guidance counselor at all. A counselor at a well-resourced district, by contrast, is much more likely to have the bandwidth to assess AI use in a draft, plus support from school infrastructure to teach ethical AI use.

This is what colleges are forgetting about AI: Learning how to use AI on one’s own isn’t the same thing as learning ethical AI use from a paid educator. AI literacy isn’t just about affording a ChatGPT subscription—it’s about cultural osmosis, regular integration and direct AI-proficiency training.

As our current admissions system stands, colleges’ differing AI policies inevitably prioritize the wealthy. This problem is most evident in colleges’ detection systems. As mentioned above, colleges do not typically disclose what detection software they use to screen for AI, nor how they train their admissions officers to “feel” for its use. Regardless of this nondisclosure, both of these policing systems are unreliable. Detection software is notoriously inaccurate and biased against nonnative English speakers. Human detection is also inaccurate, and dependent on each admissions officer’s own AI literacy.

And even if a student is rejected for suspected AI usage, colleges don’t have to tell them that’s what happened. Colleges don’t include justifications in their rejection letters. Because of this, colleges are allowed to reject applications that “feel” like AI, but they aren’t required to publish their training, detection rates or any other data.

In my opinion, if colleges can't prove their AI-detection methods are equitable, they have no right to penalize applicants for AI use. Colleges should be more clear: Are they using Turnitin? GPTZero? Copyleaks? Do they check for AI watermarking? How often do they discard applications for AI use? What data trains their AI-detection tools? How do they train their officers? Such disclosure would work to level the playing field for students without admissions support.

One counterargument to such disclosure is that it could teach applicants how to cheat without getting caught. But the current problem is much worse than that potential outcome. As long as AI detection is murky, essays are just another focal point for inequality and bias, and not the leveling, “holistic” metric they are meant to be. As AI continues growing in sophistication, these inequities will only grow.

Disclosing one’s behind-the-scenes approach to AI isn’t a huge ask. Colleges already demand their applicants prove their AI literacy. It’s time colleges proved theirs.

title: Girl, 15, turns bullying ordeal into mental health initiative for others
summary: Aanya Mukherjee's journey through high school was marred by bullying that took a toll on her mental health and self-esteem. After a disappointing response from her initial school, she transferred to a more supportive environment that fostered her healing. Passionate about mental health, she founded a nonprofit and advocates for the inclusion of youth perspectives in these vital discussions.
full_text:
Her experience highlights why parents and schools need to take bullying seriously and make children feel heard.

For many teenagers, school is more than a place to attend classes. It is where they build friendships, discover who they are and begin to understand where they belong. But when bullying enters that space, it can affect much more than a child's experience of school. It can shake their confidence, affect their mental health and leave them feeling isolated, even when they are surrounded by people. For 17-year-old Aanya Mukherjee from California, this was not just a possibility. It was something she experienced herself. What makes her story particularly relevant for parents is what she chose to do afterwards: she started working towards making mental health support more accessible to other teenagers, while ensuring young people have a voice in conversations about their well-being.

28 Sept 2026 | 08:18

Does your teenager tell you about their friends, or do you often have to ask? How much do you know about their social life?

In an interview with People, Aanya recalled how alone she felt during the period when she was being bullied. “I felt very isolated when it happened to me. I didn't think I would make any friends and I didn't think it would ever end,” she said. “But it did.” Her experience offers parents an important reminder: children may not always tell adults what they are going through, and the effects of bullying may reach far beyond what is immediately visible.

When bullying begins to affect a child's sense of self

According to People, Aanya faced rumours, false stories about her and her family, harassment and, at times, stalking during her early high school years. She said the experience affected her confidence, mental health and academic performance. Her family sought help from the private school she initially attended near their home in San Jose, but Aanya said they were disappointed with the response. She eventually moved to Pinewood School in Los Altos, where she is now a student. Her experience highlights an important distinction for parents: bullying is not always a physical confrontation that teachers or parents can easily see. It can also take the form of social exclusion, rumours, repeated humiliation and harassment through digital platforms. A child who is being targeted may become reluctant to attend school, withdraw from friends or appear unusually anxious. Some children may become irritable, struggle to concentrate or show changes in their academic performance. None of these signs automatically means bullying is taking place, but a noticeable change in behaviour is worth exploring with care. For parents, the first step is not necessarily to find an immediate solution. It is to make it easier for a child to speak honestly about what is happening.

Aanya Mukherjee turned her experience of bullying into an initiative to support other teenagers.

Why listening matters more than parents may realise

When children share a difficult experience, adults may instinctively try to fix it. They might tell them to ignore the other children, stand up for themselves or focus on their studies. Although such responses may come from a place of concern, they can leave a child feeling that the seriousness of their experience has not been understood. Aanya's story highlights the importance of taking a young person's account seriously. She said her experience made her more interested in how schools address bullying and student well-being, particularly because the support she had sought had not worked in her favour. A turning point came when a mental health counsellor encouraged her to “be a leader in your own life”. That advice helped her move towards taking an active role in improving support for other teenagers. This does not mean a child should be expected to solve bullying independently. Rather, parents can help them regain a sense of agency while making it clear that adults are responsible for helping keep them safe. A useful starting point is to listen without interrupting, ask what happened and acknowledge how the child feels. Parents can then work with the school to understand the situation and identify practical steps to prevent further harassment. If bullying is affecting a child's emotional well-being, professional support may also be appropriate.

Turning a painful experience into support for other teens

Aanya began working with groups of educators, parents and mental health professionals to explore ways to help teenagers facing similar challenges. However, she noticed something missing from many discussions about young people's mental health: young people themselves. “It was strange that adults were having all these conversations about what teenagers needed, but teenagers themselves weren't necessarily being included,” she told People. That observation eventually led her to start Buy Yourself Flowers, a teen-led nonprofit focused on mental health awareness and involving young people in the conversation about their well-being. One of its initiatives is the distribution of “bloom boxes”, small mental health toolkits containing items such as herbal teas, candles, affirmations, mini journals, face masks and a list of support resources. Aanya said the organisation had distributed around 500 boxes to schools in the area. She also helps organise workshops led by teenagers and has started a podcast. The idea is not that a box of comforting items can resolve bullying or replace professional help. Instead, the initiative offers one way to open up conversations about mental health and remind young people that support is available. Aanya believes peer-led workshops can help teenagers connect through shared experiences. Reflecting on her own isolation, she told People: “It sounds cliche, but it brings home that you're not alone.” Her initiative also illustrates why teenagers should be included in conversations about their own needs. Parents and teachers may have the experience to guide them, but listening to young people can help adults better understand the pressures they face, particularly online.

What parents can learn from Aanya's experience

One of the most important lessons is that bullying should not be dismissed as a normal part of growing up. Telling children that everyone goes through it may unintentionally suggest that they have to endure it without asking for help. Parents can begin by creating regular opportunities for honest conversations, rather than waiting until a problem becomes overwhelming. Asking open questions about friendships, school and online interactions can make it easier for children to share concerns in their own time. It is also important to take cyberbullying seriously. Aanya told People that social media can make harassment difficult to escape because rumours and private conversations can spread quickly. She advises teenagers to report cyberbullying to school administrators early rather than simply hoping it will stop. Parents can help by keeping records of threatening or harassing messages, reporting incidents through the appropriate school or platform channels and avoiding responses that might expose the child to further humiliation. Schools should be involved when the behaviour involves students or affects a child's safety and ability to learn. Above all, children need to know that asking for help is not a sign of weakness. Parents do not have to possess all the answers; they need to show that they are willing to listen, take action and stay alongside their child as they work through the situation. Aanya's experience is a reminder that recovery does not happen simply because a child changes schools or learns to ignore hurtful comments. Feeling safe, rebuilding confidence and finding supportive relationships can take time. As she reflected on her own experience, she offered a message to other teenagers: “It's possible to move on. At the end of the day, you are in charge of your own life.” For parents, the lesson is to help children believe that they are not defined by how others treat them - and to ensure they do not have to face bullying alone.

End of Article

title: International security and defence: Is it time for universities to step up?
summary:
In her latest column for The PIE, Diana Beech asks whether universities can keep their doors open to the world while guarding against growing security threats – and why getting that balance right has never mattered more.

The post International security and defence: Is it time for universities to step up? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Speaking at the International Dialogue on Education (ID-E) conference in Berlin on 30 September, I was struck by how fundamentally the conversation about universities and national security has changed in the past year.

What was once a niche discussion about research governance and international partnerships has become a frontline policy challenge for higher education leaders across the Western world.

Representing the UK, I joined colleagues from the US, Finland and Germany to grapple with the question of how universities can prepare for emerging security threats while remaining open, international and committed to academic freedom.

A growing policy challenge

The timing of the discussion could not have been more relevant. On the same day as we were meeting in the Felleshus Berlin, MI5 had warned that more than 100 UK-linked academics had contributed to projects funded by a Chinese research institute alleged to support espionage activities.

This prompted UK ministers to urge universities to exercise greater vigilance over their international activities, highlighting how universities have become both strategic assets and critical battlegrounds in the race for global dominance.

As geopolitical tensions deepen, Western governments are paying closer attention to the role universities play in developing new technologies, protecting sensitive research and cultivating the talent on which future prosperity and security depend.

The nature of defence has changed too. National resilience today relies not only on military capability but also on advanced skills, scientific expertise and technological innovation. Cyber security, artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technologies and surveillance systems all draw heavily on knowledge generated within universities.

Universities educate the engineers designing future defence technologies, they train the cyber specialists protecting critical infrastructure and they conduct essential research in relevant and emerging fields.

At the same time, they are expected to preserve the openness that underpins academic inquiry and sustain the international networks that help societies anticipate and respond to complex global challenges.

Whether they are comfortable with the idea or not, universities have become an integral part of our national resilience infrastructure.

A licence to operate?

While universities are unlikely to be taking on James Bond’s mantle any time soon, I told colleagues in Berlin that Britain’s most famous fictional spy may provide a useful analogy for their situation.

‘Agent 007’ possesses a licence to kill, granted by the state and exercised on its behalf in the interests of national security. Universities operate under a different but equally important licence, whereby society grants them the freedom to educate, research, innovate and challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of the public good.

Yet, like Bond’s, that licence is not unconditional and can be revoked if future political masters are unconvinced by their offering to the nation.

In the UK, institutional autonomy depends on public confidence that universities are acting responsibly and serving wider societal interests. With this freedom comes an obligation to manage risk, safeguard sensitive knowledge wherever necessary and ensure international engagement is undertaken with care and judgement.

This does not mean universities should become agents of the state, but demonstrating their value in areas that matter to the public is one of the strongest ways institutions can maintain legitimacy and trust.

International engagement remains vital

Cutting themselves off from international engagement is just not an option for universities today. Institutions that isolate themselves from global networks are likely to become less innovative, less competitive and ultimately less resilient.

Internationally mobile staff and students broaden institutional expertise and deepen cultural understanding on campus. In the same way, global research partnerships provide access to knowledge that no single nation can generate alone. So, the challenge facing universities today is how to continue being international responsibly, not stopping engagement altogether.

As security concerns rise, international activities require robust governance, effective due diligence and mature risk management. University managers and their governors must understand who they are working with, where vulnerabilities may exist and how risks can be mitigated without closing off vital opportunities for collaboration.

The cyber frontier

The key is not to get fixated on physical mobility alone. As our higher education institutions become more globally connected, they become more exposed to cyber-attacks, data theft and attempts to access sensitive research and intellectual property.

Addressing these risks requires investment, expertise and the sustained attention of university executives. Governors, too, need to ensure they are building institutions capable of anticipating disruption, adapting quickly and continuing to operate effectively when challenges arise.

Finding the right balance

While the discussion in Berlin was wide-ranging, my overriding takeaway was that universities must resist allowing legitimate security concerns to evolve into a culture of suspicion.

The purpose of higher education is to bring people, ideas and cultures together and, if security measures become so restrictive that they undermine collaboration and academic exchange, we risk weakening the very qualities that make universities valuable in the first place.

Perfect security will never be achievable for institutions whose mission depends on openness and engagement. The task for university leaders, therefore, is to navigate the delicate space between protecting what matters to the country and preserving what matters to their mission.

In an increasingly uncertain world, universities do not need to choose between openness and security. They need to uphold both – not by closing doors, but by ensuring they remain open safely.

full_text:
October 12, 2026, by Dean Hoke: Is the international student pipeline to American colleges shrinking, or is the way students choose where to study fundamentally changing? That question was at the center of our October 6 Small College America: Consequential Conversations webinar, which I co-hosted with W. Kent Barnds of Augustana College.

We were joined by three guests who brought national leadership, journalistic insight, and firsthand experience to the discussion. Dr. Fanta Aw, Executive Director and CEO of NAFSA (Association of International Educators), offered a national and global perspective. Karin Fischer, international reporter for The Chronicle of Higher Education, brought more than two decades of reporting on international education. And Liz Nino, Executive Director of International Enrollment at Augustana College, brought the perspective of someone on the front lines—traveling internationally, meeting students and families, and navigating today’s recruitment challenges.

The conversation revealed a complicated picture, but also some reasons for optimism.

Is Student Interest Declining, or Are the Obstacles Growing?

Karin Fischer described today’s international enrollment environment as one of “permanent uncertainty.” Visa difficulties, shifting government policies, and concerns about post-graduation opportunities are complicating decisions for students and families.

Liz Nino highlighted these challenges through Augustana’s recruitment experience. Students who wanted to attend an American college sometimes couldn’t get visas or even schedule interviews in time.

That raises an important question: Are American colleges losing their appeal, or are students simply finding it harder to get here?

The Small College Advantage

Much of the national conversation focuses on large research universities, but smaller institutions face different circumstances. Our panelists explored how personal relationships, residential experiences, and a sense of community can give small colleges competitive advantages. Yet those strengths mean little if international students and their families don’t understand what makes an American small college distinctive.

The discussion also went beyond enrollment numbers and tuition revenue. What happens to the educational experience when international students become a smaller part of campus life?

A Strategic Decision That Could Shape the Next Decade

Perhaps the most consequential advice came from Fanta Aw, who cautioned college leaders against allowing today’s difficulties to dictate tomorrow’s strategy. “Don’t make a long-term strategic decision based solely on a disruption now.”

“Don’t make a long-term strategic decision based solely on a disruption now.”

Her observation raises a difficult question for presidents and trustees: How do you manage immediate financial pressures without sacrificing international relationships and recruitment networks that took years to establish? The panelists also explored opportunities that may be emerging despite today’s challenges, including alternative pathways for international students.

We concluded by asking each panelist to look five years ahead. Their perspectives offered important considerations for college leaders making decisions today.

The future of international enrollment at America’s small colleges may depend less on the size of their recruitment budgets than on the strategic choices they make now.

These highlights only scratch the surface of a wide-ranging conversation. I encourage you to watch or listen to the full program and hear directly from our three panelists.

Watch the full webinar: https://youtu.be/E78DseQwp0I

Listen to the conversation: https://smallcollegeamerica.transistor.fm/51

Small College America: Consequential Conversations is a monthly discussion series hosted by Dean Hoke and W. Kent Barnds that examines the issues shaping the future of America’s small colleges.

full_text:
Private elementary school can be as expensive as college.

For parents expecting early schooling to cost less, the cost can be surprising. We compared published private elementary-school tuition.

We ranked these private elementary schools by published tuition costs for kindergartners at independent day schools with general academic programs for 2026–27.

When one rate covers several grades, we used the kindergarten rate. Costs do not include optional programs, one-time fees, boarding costs, or special-needs programs.

Figures represent the published kindergarten tuition at each school. We ranked schools based on their kindergarten tuition and resolved any ties alphabetically. All 25 schools in this ranking are in New York City.

This ranking is not a comprehensive national survey.

The tuition listed is the school’s sticker price, though some families pay less through financial aid.

25

City and Country School Charges $66,075

New York, New York

City and Country School’s 2026–27 tuition is $66,075 for kindergarten through second grade.1

Before deciding if it suits your child, explore the school’s approach to education. City and Country School offers financial aid, starting in kindergarten.

Aid may reduce the amount you pay. Visit City and Country School and sit in on a class. City and Country School is a progressive private school that has an active-learning curriculum that changes as its students get older.2

24

Berkeley Carroll School Charges $66,090

Brooklyn, New York

Berkeley Carroll, a private school with an arts program,4 charges $66,090 for pre-K in Brooklyn for 2026–27.3

The same rate covers kindergarten through grade twelve. That’s only $15 more than City and Country.

Tuition is only part of the cost.

Factor in transportation, after-school care, and fees. Many private schools offer need-based financial aid that may lower the net cost for qualifying families.

23

The Buckley School Charges $66,500

New York, New York

Tuition for 2026–27 is $66,500.5 Financial aid awards at Buckley range in size and some cover full tuition. Buckley’s Financial Aid Program can reduce costs for qualifying families.

Consider the aid award, Buckley’s all-boys’ program through Class IV,6 and the classroom environment for your son.

The stated tuition includes lunch, books and supplies, activities, and some athletic uniforms.

22

Trevor Day School Charges $67,500

New York, New York

Kindergarten tuition is $67,500 for 2026–27.7

Grades one through four cost $68,982. Kindergarten is the basis for this ranking.

At Trevor, it’s students’ questions that guide learning in all subject areas.8 Tuition includes field trips, books and other classroom materials, meals and the everyday incidentals. Computers, needed in the upper grades, cost extra.

Ask about the balance of inquiry- and project-based learning, direct instruction and play and decide if it’s the right approach for your child.

21

Horace Mann School Charges $68,700

Bronx, New York

Horace Mann School’s full-day tuition is $68,700 for 2026–27, covering the full-day Threes program through twelfth grade.910 Horace Mann School is tied with Friends Seminary in this tuition comparison.

Horace Mann School offers financial assistance for eligible families based on need, including full-tuition awards.

Before enrolling, check their policies on financial assistance. Eligibility depends on more than income.

Check costs that may be added to tuition.

20

Friends Seminary Charges $68,700

New York, New York

Friends Seminary charges $68,700 for kindergarten through grade twelve in 2026–27, tied with Horace Mann.11

Explore Friends’ Lower School program.12 The Friends Seminary published tuition includes fees, books, breakfast, lunch, and required trips.

However, there could be a one-time fee for entering students, so year one might cost more.

Ask for a detailed written list of what’s included in daily costs, as well as likely additional costs, before accepting a school’s admission offer. Friends offers financial assistance on expenses above and beyond tuition for some optional activities.

19

Bank Street School for Children Charges $68,885

New York, New York

The tuition for Bank Street’s kindergarten-through-fourth-grade program is $68,885.13 This price includes books, field trips, activities and materials. Costs not included in tuition are lunch, early-morning care, after-school programs, and a parent-association fee.

Two schools with similar tuition may charge differently for extras.

Bank Street offers financial aid, which may lower a qualifying family’s cost. Bank Street’s philosophy emphasizes the child’s developmental stage, hands-on learning, and relationship building.14

18

Columbia Grammar & Preparatory School Charges $68,910

New York, New York

Columbia Grammar & Preparatory School’s K–8 tuition is $68,910 for 2026–27.15

Tuition includes books, meals, trips, athletics, and required activity fees. The kindergarten program includes small-group reading, phonological awareness, and cross-curricular learning.16

Ask about transportation and care costs. Columbia offers need-based financial assistance from kindergarten, so ask about your family’s net cost. Columbia Grammar & Preparatory School is $25 more than Bank Street.

17

Birch Wathen Lenox School Charges $69,000

New York, New York

Birch Wathen Lenox School’s tuition18 is $69,000 for the 2026–27 school year (excluding its separate EXCEL program).17

Tuition includes supplies, books and most field trips. Other costs may include transportation, certain field trips, and after-school activities and programs.

Birch Wathen Lenox School offers financial aid.

Financial aid is typically focused on students applying to the school at its main entry grades (including kindergarten). Ask about financial aid in different grades, where availability may be limited.

Consider affordability as your child progresses through school.

16

The Brearley School Charges $69,600

New York, New York

Tuition for all grade levels at Brearley School is $69,600.19

An expensive price tag does not establish a better education. Check which expenses tuition covers and whether activities or transportation cost extra.

Use Brearley School’s financial aid calculator to get an estimate, but an estimate does not guarantee an award.

Brearley is an all-girls’ private school serving kindergarten through Class XII. Its Lower School describes an academic program that encourages a love of learning and community engagement.20

15

The Hewitt School Charges $69,990

New York, New York

At Hewitt School,22 tuition is $69,990 for the 2026–27 school year.21 That covers kindergarten through grade twelve. Meals, books, technology, field trips and some transportation costs are included in tuition.

Summer programs and after-school programs are an additional cost.

Financial aid depends on a family’s finances. If you are looking at several private schools in the area, ask what costs and resources are included, and what financial aid is available at each one.

14

Léman Manhattan Preparatory School Charges $70,700

New York, New York

Léman Manhattan Preparatory School’s 2026–27 tuition is $70,700 for kindergarten through grade twelve.23

This is the published day-school rate, not a boarding cost. When determining costs, don’t take tuition at face value.

Ask each private school for a written fee schedule that lays out all expenses including optional programs before you visit. You shouldn’t assume you’ll qualify for need-based financial aid or sibling discounts, but ask. Tuition comparisons can miss differences in programs and included costs.

The goal of Léman Manhattan Preparatory School Lower School is an education focused on nurturing the “total development, academic, social, and emotional, of the young child.”24

13

Marymount School of New York Charges $70,750

New York, New York

Marymount School of New York’s tuition is $70,750 for kindergarten through grade twelve for the 2026–27 school year.25 Once you receive an acceptance, compare the options and see which is the right fit for your family – commute, culture, and classroom approach.

Cost matters too.

This is a Catholic girls’ school and offers Spanish starting in kindergarten in its Lower School program.26 Financial aid may reduce this amount.

Apply and share your financial information to learn your net cost. This is the full sticker price of the school. This is $50 more expensive than the sticker price tuition at Léman for kindergarten, but $50 likely wouldn’t make or break your decision on which school to attend.

12

The Dalton School Charges $70,800

New York, New York

Dalton’s tuition is $70,800, just $50 more than Marymount.27

Ask questions about the Dalton Plan and the three pillars: House, Assignment and Lab.28 Dalton hopes to meet the full demonstrated need of all students admitted to each grade.

In kindergarten, ask how those pieces work in daily lessons.

Your child’s needs and the financial aid offer may matter more than a small tuition difference. Dalton’s tuition is a package that includes books, lunches, trips and more.

Parents’ Association dues are charged separately.

11

Convent of the Sacred Heart Charges $70,850

New York, New York

Kindergarten-through-grade-twelve tuition is $70,850 for the 2026–27 academic year.29

That is slightly more than Dalton’s tuition, but the difference does not establish educational quality. Consider whether Sacred Heart fits your child.

Parents should review Sacred Heart’s mission statement, particularly its Catholic and Sacred Heart principles,30 and consider whether they suit your family’s expectations and daily life.

Pre-kindergarten and junior kindergarten cost less. Check the tuition page for details.

There is financial aid for eligible families.

10

Ethical Culture Fieldston School Charges $70,890

New York, New York (Manhattan) and Bronx, New York

Ethical Culture Fieldston School’s 2026–27 tuition is $70,890.31

Lunch, textbooks, the yearbook, and student accident insurance are included. There is also financial aid available for families that may need assistance.

Ethical Culture Fieldston’s Lower Divisions operate in Manhattan and the Bronx as parts of one school.32

Visit the early-grade locations and compare their commute and atmosphere.

9

The Chapin School Charges $71,000

New York, New York

Chapin’s 2026–27 tuition for kindergarten through Class XII is $71,000.33 Chapin’s Lower School includes units on families and community.34 A visit can show how children collaborate.

There are other expenses associated with attending Chapin.

Financial aid is offered at all grade levels for qualifying families. Extra fees cover items such as parent-association dues and (in higher grades) laptops.

Don’t sign on the dotted line based on the tuition alone, and estimate your family’s total cost for the first year at Chapin before you commit.

8

The Spence School Charges $71,185

New York, New York

Spence School’s tuition for 2026–27 is $71,185.35 Before writing off a school because of cost, investigate dismissal times for kindergartners, aftercare costs, and other extras.

Tuition includes program costs and is the same across grades. Need-based financial aid may reduce your cost. To assess classroom quality,36 ask what attention a struggling or gifted student would receive.

Tuition alone cannot answer that.

7

Riverdale Country School Charges $71,350

Bronx, New York

Tuition is $71,350 for 2026–27 at Riverdale’s Lower School, serving pre-K through fifth grade.37 Tuition includes lunch, books, and required activities.

The program includes two teachers in each classroom and support from literacy and math specialists.38

After-school care and transportation are not included. Consider those costs, commute time, and the financial aid package.

6

Trinity School Charges $71,500

New York, New York

Trinity School’s published tuition is $71,500 for the 2026–27 school year, before any additional costs.39 Ask for a breakdown of additional expenses, including specialty programs and after-hours child care. There is financial aid based on need.

On its Lower School webpage, Trinity mentions the importance of attending to the social, physical, emotional and cognitive development of students from the start of kindergarten.40

The program emphasizes the whole child. See for yourself how this plays out in the classroom.

When choosing a school, consider more than status.

Factor in commute time, financial aid and your child’s needs.

5

Grace Church School Charges $71,570

New York, New York

Grace Church School’s published tuition for junior kindergarten and kindergarten in 2026–27 is $71,570.41 Sticker price doesn’t always tell the whole story. Some schools will include things in their tuition while others charge separately.

Research the kindergarten program before deciding.

Junior kindergarten and kindergarten are staffed with head and associate teachers.42 Grace Church School offers need-based aid.

Grace Church School also has a program in downtown Manhattan that extends all the way up to grade twelve although this ranking uses kindergarten tuition.

Check whether after-school care, lunches, technology and activity fees are extra at Grace Church School.

4

The Nightingale-Bamford School Charges $71,665

New York, New York

title: CHE Ranking 2027: Studierendenbefragung beginnt
summary: Vom 12. Oktober 2026 bis zum 07. Februar 2027 haben Studierende wieder die Gelegenheit, im Rahmen der Studierendenbefragung für das CHE Hochschulranking...
full_text:
Vom 12. Oktober 2026 bis zum 07. Februar 2027 haben Studierende wieder die Gelegenheit, im Rahmen der Studierendenbefragung für das CHE Hochschulranking ihre Studienbedingungen zu bewerten. Für das CHE Ranking 2027 werden die Daten in den Fächern Mathematik, Informatik, Biologie, Chemie, Biochemie, Geografie, Geowissenschaften, Physik, Medizin, Zahnmedizin, Pharmazie, Pflege/Pflegewissenschaft, Sport/Sportwissenschaft, Soziologie und Politikwissenschaft/Sozialwissenschaft aktualisiert. In diesem Jahr neu dabei sind die Studienbereiche Kommunikationswissenschaft/Journalistik sowie das Lehramt an Grundschulen. Darüber hinaus haben die Hochschulen auch die Möglichkeit, weitere Studiengänge aus diesem Fächerspektrum mit in die Untersuchung einbeziehen zu lassen.

Pädagogische Hochschulen erstmals einbezogen

Befragt werden Studierenden in den grundständigen Studiengängen (Staatsexamen, Bachelor oder Diplom) an Universitäten, Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften sowie an Dualen Hochschulen. Erstmalig werden auch die Studierenden an den Pädagogischen Hochschulen (PH) in Baden-Württemberg angeschrieben, die wegen der speziellen Ausrichtung der PHs auf Lehramtsstudiengänge bisher nicht am CHE Hochschulranking teilnehmen konnten.

Für die Befragung werden Studierende ab dem dritten Fachsemester bis einschließlich zwei Semester über der Regelstudienzeit einbezogen. Die Studierenden in den Masterstudiengängen für das Lehramt an Grundschulen werden ebenfalls zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt befragt, die Studierenden der übrigen Studiengänge ab Mitte Januar 2027 bis Ende Juli 2027.

Die Einladungen zur Befragung versenden die Hochschulen direkt an ihre jeweiligen Studierenden. Die Studierenden können wichtige Aspekte des Studiums bewerten: z. B. die Studienorganisation, die Betreuung durch Lehrende oder die Unterstützung im Studium. In vielen Fächern gibt es auch fachspezifische Fragen, wie zum Beispiel zur Examensvorbereitung im Fach Pharmazie oder zu den Laborpraktika in naturwissenschaftlichen Fächern. Der Fragebogen umfasst zudem spezielle Fragen zur Nutzung von Künstlicher Intelligenz im Studium.

„Eine hohe Beteiligung an der Studierendenbefragung ist sehr wichtig, damit eine ausreichende Zahl an Bewertungen für die statistische Auswertung zur Verfügung steht. Denn bei zu geringen Rücklaufzahlen können die Ergebnisse für einzelne Hochschulen nicht im CHE Hochschulranking ausgewiesen werden und es fehlen den Studieninteressierten wichtige Informationen als Grundlage ihrer Hochschulwahl“, sagt Luisa Weiser, im CHE Hochschulranking zuständig für die Studierendenbefragung.

Faktenerhebung läuft bereits

Seit Anfang September läuft bereits die Faktenerhebung bei den Organisationseinheiten wie Fakultäten, Fachbereichen, Instituten und Lehrkräftebildungszentren, die in das CHE Ranking 2027 einbezogenen Studiengänge anbieten. Hier werden insbesondere eine Vielzahl struktureller Informationen über die Studienangebote, Zahlen zu Studierenden und Studienabschlüssen sowie beschreibende Texte zu den Besonderheiten des Studiums an der jeweiligen Hochschule erhoben. Die Fragebögen sind noch bis Ende Oktober geöffnet, bevor das CHE sie im November schließt und durchsieht, um sie dann den Hochschulen noch einmal bis Mitte Januar für Korrekturen und Ergänzungen zur Verfügung zu stellen.

Die Ergebnisse werden Anfang Mai 2027 im ZEIT Studienführer sowie online unter heystudium.de/ranking veröffentlicht.
